summary: Daniel 11 continues an angelic disclosure by tracing a long sequence of rulers, wars, alliances, betrayals, and reversals. The chapter moves from Persia and Greece into repeated conflict between a king of the south and a king of the north, then focuses on a contemptible ruler who attacks the holy covenant, profanes the sanctuary, and exalts himself before coming to an unsupported end.
whyItMatters: This chapter is one of Daniel’s most detailed visions of imperial conflict and persecution. In the book’s larger movement, it frames violent political power as real but bounded by “the appointed time.”

context.author: The visions speak in Daniel’s first-person setting, but the book does not name a final editor; traditional and critical readers differ on authorship.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: The story world reaches from the Babylonian exile into Persian rule; many scholars date the final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167–164 BC, while traditional readings place authorship with the sixth-century Daniel.
context.setting: The book is set in Babylonian and Persian courts, while the later visions reach toward the persecution associated with Antiochus IV Epiphanes.
context.literaryForm: Apocalyptic vision with angelic disclosure, using historical sequence, symbolic timing, and compressed descriptions of rulers and conflicts.

outline.heading: Persia, Greece, and a divided kingdom
outline.note: The speaker strengthens Darius, announces coming Persian kings, then describes a mighty king whose kingdom is broken and divided.

outline.heading: North and south begin their struggle
outline.note: The king of the south and the king of the north enter cycles of alliance, betrayal, invasion, plunder, return, and renewed war.

outline.heading: The northern ruler gains the upper hand
outline.note: The conflict widens; armies rise and fall, the glorious land is entered, a ruler stumbles, and another tax-raising figure briefly stands in his place.

outline.heading: A contemptible person rises by deceit
outline.note: A new ruler obtains power by flatteries, makes treaties deceitfully, fights the king of the south, speaks lies at one table, and turns against the holy covenant.

outline.heading: The sanctuary is profaned and the wise suffer
outline.note: A later southern campaign fails, anger turns against the holy covenant, the sanctuary is profaned, the continual burnt offering is removed, and wise instructors suffer while some are refined.

outline.heading: The self-exalting king and his end
outline.note: The king magnifies himself above every god, honors a foreign god, battles at the time of the end, enters the glorious land, gains treasures, rages at troubling news, and comes to his end with no helper.

keyVerses.text: “Now I will show you the truth. Behold, three more kings will stand up in Persia. The fourth will be far richer than all of them. When he has grown strong through his riches, he will stir up all against the realm of Greece.
keyVerses.why: This verse announces the disclosure’s claim to show “the truth” and begins the chapter’s sequence of imperial powers.

keyVerses.text: “In his place a contemptible person will stand up, to whom they had not given the honor of the kingdom; but he will come in time of security, and will obtain the kingdom by flatteries.
keyVerses.why: This verse introduces the ruler who dominates much of the chapter’s second half through deceit, force, and religious hostility.

keyVerses.text: “Forces from him will profane the sanctuary, even the fortress, and will take away the continual burnt offering. Then they will set up the abomination that makes desolate.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s clearest description of direct attack on worship and the sanctuary.

keyVerses.text: He will plant the tents of his palace between the sea and the glorious holy mountain; yet he will come to his end, and no one will help him.
keyVerses.why: The chapter closes by limiting the power of the final arrogant ruler it describes.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter begins with “As for me,” continuing the disclosure scene from the surrounding vision. Inside this chapter, the speaker says he will show Daniel “the truth,” then narrates coming conflicts in compressed form. The chapter itself does not pause to identify every figure by personal name.

questions.question: Why does the chapter keep saying rulers will “stand up”?
questions.answer: “Stand up” is repeated for kings and successors who arise to power. It marks transitions in rule rather than describing a physical posture. The repeated phrase helps the reader follow the sequence of regimes and replacements.

questions.question: Who are the king of the south and the king of the north?
questions.answer: The chapter uses directional titles rather than personal names. The visions reach toward the Antiochus IV crisis, and many readers connect these north-south conflicts with Hellenistic kingdoms after Alexander. The chapter itself identifies them only by their directional titles and actions.

questions.question: What is “the glorious land”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears when a conquering ruler stands there and again when a later ruler enters it. The chapter does not define the phrase, but in Daniel’s setting it points to the land bound up with Daniel’s people and worship. Readers should avoid importing more detail than the chapter gives.

questions.question: What is the “holy covenant”?
questions.answer: The phrase names what the hostile ruler opposes and what some people forsake. In the chapter, it is closely tied to the sanctuary, the continual burnt offering, and the people who know their God. The text depicts pressure on Jewish worship and loyalty without reducing the issue to ordinary politics.

questions.question: What is the “abomination that makes desolate”?
questions.answer: Verse 31 says forces from the ruler profane the sanctuary, take away the continual burnt offering, and set up the abomination that makes desolate. The chapter does not define the object or act further here. Later Jewish and Christian readers connect this phrase with desecration crises, but interpretations differ about how later uses relate to Daniel 11.

questions.question: Are the wise spared from suffering?
questions.answer: No. The chapter says those who are wise instruct many, but they also fall by sword, flame, captivity, and plunder. Their suffering is described as refining and purifying, not as proof that they failed.

questions.question: Does the chapter say the arrogant king becomes all-powerful?
questions.answer: The king magnifies himself, speaks against the God of gods, and prospers for a time. But the chapter also says his prosperity lasts only until the indignation is accomplished, and it ends with him coming to his end with no one to help him. His power is depicted as dangerous but bounded.

questions.question: What does “the appointed time” do in the chapter?
questions.answer: The phrase signals that events are not portrayed as open-ended chaos. It appears when lies at one table do not prosper, when a later southern campaign returns at a set moment, and when the suffering of the wise lasts until the time appointed. The chapter does not convert that timing into a modern calendar.

glossary.def: The ruler named in the chapter’s opening setting; his historical identification remains difficult and debated.
A directional title for one side in the repeated conflicts described through much of the chapter.
A directional title for the opposing ruler or succession of rulers in the chapter’s conflict sequence.
The covenantal loyalty and worship that the hostile ruler opposes and that some people forsake.
The regular offering that verse 31 says is taken away when the sanctuary is profaned.
Persuasive or manipulative speech by which the contemptible ruler obtains power and corrupts others.
